questions.question: Explain how automatic instruments reduce human error.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain how automatic instruments reduce human error. / [CO1]
  • Automatic instruments reduce human error by minimizing direct human involvement in measurement
  • and data handling processes. They eliminate observational errors such as parallax by providing
  • precise digital readings, and they avoid mistakes in recording and calculation through built-in data
  • logging and processing systems. These instruments ensure consistent and repeatable results by
  • operating under fixed conditions, independent of human fatigue or skill level. They also respond
  • quickly to changes and enable continuous monitoring, reducing the chance of missed observations.
  • Moreover, automatic instruments remove personal bias by relying on objective measurements, thereby
  • improving the overall accuracy and reliability of results. (Any relevant three points – (3 marks)
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: What is time constant? Explain its importance in first-order instruments.
questions.solution_html:
• What is time constant? Explain its importance in first-order instruments./ [CO1]
  • The time constant is the time required for a first-order instrument to reach about 63.2% of its final
  • steady-state value after a sudden change in input. It is a measure of the speed of response of the
  • instrument. The importance of the time constant lies in its ability to indicate how quickly an
  • instrument can respond to changes in the measured quantity. A smaller time constant means a faster
  • response and better ability to track rapid changes, while a larger time constant indicates a slower
  • response and possible lag in measurement. First-order instruments are measuring devices whose
  • response to a change in input follows a first-order differential equation, meaning the rate of change of
  • the output is proportional to the difference between the current output and the final steady value.
  • When subjected to a sudden change in input, the output does not respond instantaneously but
  • approaches the final value gradually in an exponential manner. These instruments are characterized by
  • a single time constant, which determines the speed of response. (Any relevant three points – 3
  • marks)

questions.question: How is IR spectroscopy used to identify functional groups?
questions.solution_html:
• How is IR spectroscopy used to identify functional groups? / [CO3]
  • Infrared (IR) spectroscopy is used to identify functional groups based on the absorption of infrared
  • radiation, which causes vibrations of chemical bonds in a molecule. Different functional groups
  • absorb IR radiation at characteristic wavenumbers due to their specific bond strengths and atomic
  • masses. The IR spectrum displays peaks corresponding to these absorptions, and by comparing them
  • with standard values, functional groups such as –OH, –NH, C=O, and C–H can be identified. In
  • addition to the functional group region (4000–1500 cm ¹), the fingerprint region (1500–400 cm ¹) is
  • also important, as it contains a complex pattern of absorptions unique to each compound. This region
  • helps in confirming the identity of a substance by matching it with known spectra, making IR
  • spectroscopy a reliable method for both identification and structural analysis. (Any relevant three
  • points – (3 marks)
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: State Snell’s law and write its mathematical expression.
questions.solution_html:
• State Snell’s law and write its mathematical expression. / [CO4]
  • Snell’s law states that when a ray of light passes from one medium to another, the ratio of the sine of
  • the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant for a given pair of media.
  • The mathematical expression is n1Sini = n2Sinr where i is the angle of incidence, r is the angle of
  • refraction, and n1 and n2 are the refractive indices of the two media.
  • (Statement – (1.5 marks) , Mathematical expression with terms – (1.5 marks)

questions.question: What is the function of the reference material holder? [3x4 = 12]
questions.solution_html:
• What is the function of the reference material holder? / [CO4]
  • The reference material holder is used to hold a standard or reference sample (such as a blank or
  • solvent) against which the sample is compared during measurement. Its function is to account for
  • absorbance due to the solvent, container, or instrument, thereby eliminating background interference
  • and ensuring accurate results. In a double beam spectrometer, the reference material holder plays an
  • essential role by continuously comparing the reference and sample beams simultaneously. This allows
  • real-time correction of fluctuations in source intensity and instrument conditions, leading to more
  • precise, stable, and reliable measurements.
  • (Any relevant three points – (3 marks)

questions.question: Discuss the significance of S/N ratio in analytical techniques such as spectroscopy and chromatography.
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the significance of S/N ratio in analytical techniques such as spectroscopy and
  • chromatography. / [CO1]
  • Signal refers to the measurable response produced by the analyte of interest, while noise refers to
  • unwanted random fluctuations or disturbances that affect the measurement. The signal-to-noise (S/N)
  • ratio is a measure of the strength of the analytical signal relative to the background noise, and it plays
  • a crucial role in techniques such as spectroscopy and chromatography. A high S/N ratio indicates that
  • the signal is clearly distinguishable from noise, leading to more accurate and reliable results, while a
  • low S/N ratio makes detection and quantification difficult. In spectroscopy, a higher S/N ratio
  • improves the clarity of spectral peaks and enables detection of low concentrations of substances. In
  • chromatography, it enhances peak identification, resolution, and accurate integration of peak areas.
  • The S/N ratio also determines important analytical parameters such as limit of detection (LOD) and
  • limit of quantification (LOQ). Thus, improving the S/N ratio is essential for achieving high
  • sensitivity, precision, and overall analytical performance.
  • (Definition and equation – (4 marks) , Significance – (3 marks)

questions.question: What is a flicker noise? What are its characteristics? What are the methods to reduce it?
questions.solution_html:
• What is a flicker noise? What are its characteristics? What are the methods to reduce it? /
  • [CO1]
  • Flicker noise, also known as 1/f noise, is a type of electronic noise that occurs in many electrical and
  • electronic devices, especially at low frequencies. It arises due to fluctuations in the flow of charge
  • carriers, often caused by defects, impurities, or irregularities in materials and interfaces. The name 1/f
  • noise comes from the fact that its power spectral density is inversely proportional to frequency,
  • meaning it becomes more significant at lower frequencies.
  • The main characteristic of flicker noise is that its magnitude increases as the frequency decreases,
  • dominating over other types of noise such as thermal noise at low frequencies. It is present in devices
  • like transistors, resistors, and semiconductor components. Flicker noise is generally independent of
  • temperature to some extent but strongly depends on the quality of the material and manufacturing
  • process. It is more prominent in semiconductor devices due to carrier trapping and release
  • mechanisms at defect sites.
  • To reduce flicker noise, high-quality materials with fewer defects and impurities should be used
  • during fabrication. Proper device design and improved manufacturing techniques can minimize
  • imperfections that cause noise. Increasing the operating frequency can help, as flicker noise is less
  • significant at higher frequencies. Using filtering techniques to eliminate low-frequency components
  • and employing signal modulation methods such as chopper stabilization or auto-zeroing can
  • effectively reduce its impact. Additionally, maintaining stable operating conditions and using proper
  • shielding and grounding can further help in minimizing flicker noise in practical circuits.(Definition
  • with characteristics /equation – (4 marks) , Reduction methods - (3 marks)
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Write short notes on: (a) Nernst Glower (b) Globar Source.
questions.solution_html:
• Write short notes on: (a) Nernst Glower (b) Globar Source. / [CO2]
  • (a) Nernst glower is a commonly used infrared radiation source in infrared spectroscopy. It consists of
  • a small cylindrical rod made of a mixture of rare earth metal oxides such as zirconium oxide, yttrium
  • oxide, and thorium oxide. At room temperature, these oxides are non-conductors, so the glower
  • cannot conduct electricity initially. Therefore, it requires preheating using an external heater to raise
  • its temperature to a point where it becomes electrically conductive. Once it becomes conductive, an
  • electric current is passed through the rod, heating it to a high temperature of about 1000–2000 °C. At
  • this elevated temperature, it emits continuous infrared radiation over a wide wavelength range,
  • typically from about 2 to 15 µm. The emitted radiation is fairly intense and stable, making it suitable
  • for spectroscopic measurements. The Nernst glower has a relatively long operational life and provides
  • higher intensity radiation compared to some other sources in certain regions. However, it is fragile,
  • requires a preheating arrangement, and its operation is somewhat more complex due to the need for
  • temperature control and initial heating. (3.5 marks)
  • (b) Globar source is another important infrared radiation source used in infrared spectroscopy. It is
  • made of silicon carbide in the form of a rod or cylindrical element. Unlike the Nernst glower, silicon
  • carbide is electrically conductive at room temperature, so it does not require any preheating to start
  • operation. When an electric current is passed through the globar, it is heated to temperatures around
  • 1200–1500 °C, resulting in the emission of continuous infrared radiation. The radiation produced
  • covers a broad wavelength range, typically from about 2 to 20 µm. The globar source is mechanically
  • strong, robust, and easy to handle compared to the Nernst glower. It provides stable and reproducible
  • radiation and is widely used in modern infrared spectrometers because of its simplicity and reliability.
  • Although its intensity may be slightly lower than that of the Nernst glower at shorter wavelengths, it
  • has the advantage of uniform emission and longer operational stability. Additionally, it does not
  • require complex starting procedures, making it more convenient for routine laboratory use. (3.5
  • marks).

questions.question: Derive and explain the Beer–Lambert law.
questions.solution_html:
• Derive and explain the Beer–Lambert law./ [CO3]
  • Beer–Lambert law states that when a beam of monochromatic light passes through a solution, the
  • amount of light absorbed is directly proportional to the concentration of the absorbing species and the
  • path length of the medium. Mathematically, it is expressed as A = εcl, where A is the absorbance, ε is
  • the molar absorptivity, c is the concentration of the solution, and l is the path length. As the
  • concentration of the solution increases, more light is absorbed, leading to higher absorbance.
  • Similarly, an increase in the path length also results in greater absorption of light. The absorbance is
  • also related to the intensity of incident and transmitted light by the relation A = log(I /I). This law is
  • valid under conditions such as the use of monochromatic light, dilute solutions, and absence of
  • scattering or chemical changes in the solution.
  • (Statement – (3 marks) , Derivation - (4 marks)

questions.question: Define Thermal Gravimetric Analysis (TGA). Explain its principle, instrumentation and working in detail.
questions.solution_html:
• Define Thermal Gravimetric Analysis (TGA). Explain its principle, instrumentation and working
  • in detail. / [CO4]
  • Thermal Gravimetric Analysis (TGA) is a thermal analysis technique in which the mass of a
  • substance is measured as a function of temperature or time under a controlled atmosphere.
  • The principle of TGA is based on the fact that many materials undergo changes in mass when heated
  • due to processes such as decomposition, oxidation, reduction, or loss of volatile components. By
  • continuously recording the weight change as the temperature increases, information about thermal
  • stability and composition of the sample can be obtained.
  • The instrumentation of TGA mainly consists of a sensitive microbalance, a furnace, a temperature
  • programmer, a sample holder, and a gas flow system. The microbalance continuously measures the
  • weight of the sample with high precision. The furnace provides a controlled heating environment, and
  • the temperature programmer regulates the rate of temperature increase. The sample holder, usually
  • made of inert material like platinum, holds the sample. The gas flow system supplies inert or reactive
  • gases to control the atmosphere during the analysis.
  • In the working of TGA, a small amount of sample is placed in the sample holder attached to the
  • microbalance. The sample is then heated at a controlled rate in the furnace under a specified
  • atmosphere such as nitrogen, air, or oxygen. As the temperature increases, any change in mass due to
  • decomposition, evaporation, or chemical reactions is recorded continuously. The result is plotted as a
  • thermogram, which shows weight change versus temperature or time. From this curve, important
  • information such as moisture content, thermal stability, decomposition temperature, and composition
  • of the material can be determined.
  • (Principle – (2 mark) , Instrumentation - (3 marks) , Working – (2 marks) .

questions.question: Write a note on different sampling methods. [7x4 = 28]
questions.solution_html:
• Write a note on different sampling methods. / [CO3]
  • Sampling is an important step in analytical techniques, as it ensures that the portion of material taken
  • for analysis accurately represents the whole sample. Different sampling methods are used depending
  • on the nature of the material and the purpose of analysis.
  • • Random sampling involves selecting portions of the sample at random, ensuring that every
  • part has an equal chance of being chosen. It minimizes bias and is widely used when the
  • sample is homogeneous.
  • • Systematic sampling is carried out by selecting samples at regular intervals, either in time or
  • space. It is simple and useful when dealing with large bulk materials or continuous production
  • processes.
  • • Stratified sampling is used when the material is heterogeneous. The sample is divided into
  • different layers or strata, and samples are taken from each layer to ensure proper
  • representation of all components.
  • • Grab sampling involves taking a single sample at a specific time or place. It is quick and
  • convenient but may not represent the entire bulk accurately.
  • • Composite sampling is done by combining several individual samples taken from different
  • locations or times. This method provides an average representation of the entire sample and is
  • commonly used in environmental and industrial analysis.
  • (Sampling definition and importance – (2.5 marks) , Explanation of any three sampling methods
  • – (4.5 marks)
